title: Reinforcement Schedules
subtitle: Why reward density and timing matter
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating reinforcement schedules within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain reinforcement schedules without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in reinforcement schedules.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to reinforcement schedules.

sections.explainSimply: Rewards that are too rare frustrate learning; rewards that are too frequent provide little information.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Thresholds are commonly adjusted to maintain engagement while preserving contingency. Fixed, adaptive and percentile-based rules each alter the learning environment.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Schedule design should be prespecified where possible. Automatic thresholding may stabilise reward rate but can obscure whether the underlying signal changed.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A driving instructor who gives immediate dashboard feedback while the learner practises a controllable skill.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand reinforcement schedules to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not confuse a stable reward rate with successful training.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using reinforcement schedules predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not confuse a stable reward rate with successful training. Evidence classification: established behavioural principle; implementation-dependent.

Artifact is irrelevant once feedback begins

quizBank.question: How should the evidence for Reinforcement Schedules be communicated?
